sections.b: Isaiah tells Hezekiah's story in nearly the same words as 2 Kings 18–20, but with a different shape. Isaiah leaves out Hezekiah's surrender and tribute (2 Kings 18:14–16), so the king's trust in the LORD is unbroken. The Rabshakeh confronts him at the very place where Ahaz refused Isaiah's sign (7:3; 36:2), and Hezekiah does what Ahaz would not: he goes to the temple, sends to the prophet and prays (37:1–4, 14–20). His sickness, prayer and healing (38:1–8) and his psalm of thanks (38:9–20, found only in Isaiah) mirror the city's own rescue. Chapter 39 ends the story on a darker note: he shows his treasures to Babylon's envoys, and Isaiah foretells the exile. In the book's order, Hezekiah is the model of trust between the warnings of 28–35 and the comfort of 40–66.

common: Hezekiah is remembered as one of Judah's most faithful kings, whose prayer was answered with Jerusalem's rescue and his own healing.
uncommon: Some interpreters read his last words in 39:8 as selfish indifference to his descendants' fate.

sections.b: Isaiah 31–37 traces Assyria from threat to ruin. The prophet warns that Egypt cannot save Judah from it (31:1–3), but promises that "Assyria will fall by a sword, not a man's" (31:8). The last woe of chapters 28–33 is aimed at the plunderer who broke faith (33:1, 8), and the officials who counted Jerusalem's towers will be a memory (33:18–19). In chapters 36–37 the Rabshakeh boasts that no god has rescued any land from Assyria; Isaiah answers that Assyria's conquests were the LORD's plan from long ago (37:26), and the angel of the LORD strikes its camp (37:36). Sennacherib's own annals confirm the campaign of 701 and his failure to take Jerusalem, and the Lachish reliefs show what his army did to Judah's towns.

common: Isaiah taught that Assyria was the LORD's tool to punish Judah, but that it would itself be judged for its pride.

sections.b: Isaiah's last woes repeat his warning against the alliance with Egypt: "Woe to those going down to Egypt for help" (31:1). Egypt is human, not God, and its horses are flesh, not spirit (31:3). The Rabshakeh, of all people, makes the same point, calling Egypt a crushed reed that pierces the hand that leans on it (36:6). The book closes the Hezekiah story with another alliance: envoys from Merodach-baladan of Babylon, probably seeking a partner in revolt, are shown the king's whole arsenal (39:1–2). Isaiah's response is the first prophecy in the book that Babylon will carry off Judah's treasures and sons (39:6–7). In Isaiah, trusting foreign powers is the opposite of trusting the LORD.

Isaiah 34 singles Edom out among the nations for the LORD's sword. The slaughter is pictured as a sacrifice at Bozrah, Edom's capital (34:6), the land burns like Sodom (34:9–10), and it is measured out for "shapelessness" and "emptiness," the chaos of Genesis 1:2 (34:11). Owls, jackals, a goat-demon and Lilith take it over (34:11–15). The reason is not stated, but Edom's part in Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10–14) lies behind most readings. Isaiah 63:1–6 returns to the scene, with the LORD coming from Bozrah in red-stained clothes. In later Jewish interpretation Edom came to stand for Rome.
sections.refs: Isaiah 34:5–17; Isaiah 63:1–6; Isaiah 21:11–12; Obadiah 10–14; Psalm 137:7; Malachi 1:2–4

sections.b: In Isaiah 31–37 the LORD defends Zion. He is like a lion that will not let go of its prey and like birds hovering over a nest; he will "pass over" Jerusalem as on the night of the exodus (31:4–5). His fire is in Zion (31:9), and it tests the city's own sinners (33:14). Zion will be "a tent no one will pack up," guarded by the LORD as by broad rivers (33:20–21). In chapter 37 Daughter Zion laughs at Sennacherib (37:22), and the LORD promises that the Assyrian will not enter the city or shoot an arrow at it (37:33–35). The rescue of 701 made this one of the strongest themes of Isaiah's tradition, and Jeremiah later had to warn that the temple was no guarantee (Jeremiah 7:4).
sections.refs: Isaiah 31:4–9; Isaiah 33:14–24; Isaiah 37:22–35; Psalm 46; Psalm 48; Jeremiah 7:4

sections.h: Hezekiah at the gates of Sheol
sections.b: Hezekiah's psalm (Isaiah 38:9–20) is one of the Bible's fullest pictures of Sheol as a sick man feared it. He feels himself marched off "into the gates of Sheol" in the middle of life (38:10), to a place where he will not see Yah "in the land of the living" (38:11). Sheol gives God no thanks, death does not praise him, and those who go down to the pit cannot hope in his faithfulness (38:18), a thought shared with Psalms 6:5, 30:9, 88:10–12 and 115:17. Praise belongs to the living (38:19). Christians differ on what such verses say about the dead between death and resurrection; see the card on Isaiah 38.
sections.refs: Isaiah 38:10–20; Psalm 6:5; Psalm 30:9; Psalm 88:10–12; Psalm 115:17; Matthew 16:18

sections.b: Isaiah joins healing with forgiveness. The vision of Zion ends: "And none who live there will say, 'I am sick'; / the people who dwell in it will have their guilt lifted away" (33:24). In chapter 35 the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame leap and the mute sing (35:5–6), the signs Jesus pointed to in Matthew 11:5. In chapter 38 Hezekiah's healing comes with a remedy of pressed figs (38:21) and with the confession that God has flung all his sins behind his back (38:17). Healing in these chapters is God's gift of new life, of body and of people together.
sections.refs: Isaiah 33:24; Isaiah 35:5–6; Isaiah 38:1–21; Psalm 103:3; Matthew 11:5; Mark 7:32–37

sections.h: The angel who struck Assyria's camp
sections.b: "The angel of the LORD went out and struck the camp of Assyria: one hundred eighty-five thousand" (Isaiah 37:36, as in 2 Kings 19:35). The verb is the one used for the destroyer who struck Egypt's firstborn (Exodus 12:23) and for the angel who struck Israel in David's day (2 Samuel 24:16). Isaiah had promised that Assyria would fall "by a sword, not a man's" (31:8). Herodotus tells an Egyptian story of Sennacherib's army undone in one night by mice (Histories 2.141), and Josephus calls it a plague.
sections.refs: Isaiah 37:36; 2 Kings 19:35; Isaiah 31:8; Exodus 12:23; 2 Samuel 24:16; 2 Chronicles 32:21

sections.b: Isaiah 34:14 names two creatures of the ruins that later readers took as demons: the sa'ir, literally "hairy one," which the site renders "goat-demon" as at 13:21 (some take it as a plain wild goat), and whose plural in Leviticus 17:7 names the "goat idols" Israel sacrificed to, and lilit, Lilith, a female night demon known from Mesopotamian texts. The Greek translates with "demons" and "donkey-centaurs," the Latin with lamia, and the KJV with "satyr" and "screech owl." The Great Isaiah Scroll has the plural "liliths," and the Songs of the Sage from Qumran list liliths among spirits to be driven away. Later Jewish legend made Lilith Adam's first wife, but none of that is in Isaiah, who uses her to say that ruined Edom will belong to the creatures of the night.

sections.h: The day of vengeance in Isaiah 34–35
sections.b: Isaiah 34:8 calls the judgment on Edom "the LORD's day of vengeance, / a year of paying back, to win Zion's case." The same pairing of a day and a year returns in 61:2 and 63:4, and chapter 35 gives its other side: "Vengeance is coming, / God's repayment. / He is coming himself to save you" (35:4). The cosmic signs of 34:4, the army of heaven rotting and the sky rolled up like a scroll, are taken up in Matthew 24:29 and Revelation 6:13–14. Readers differ on whether the language describes the literal end of the world, a political collapse, or both.
sections.refs: Isaiah 34:1–17; Isaiah 35:4; Isaiah 61:2; Isaiah 63:4; Matthew 24:29; Revelation 6:13–14

sections.b: Isaiah 35 answers the ruin of chapter 34 and the withering of 33:9. The wilderness blooms like the crocus and receives the glory of Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon (35:1–2), water breaks out in the desert and the mirage becomes a pond (35:6–7), and a holy road leads the ransomed home to Zion (35:8–10). The theme began in 32:15, where a spirit from on high turns the wilderness into garden land, and it runs on through 41:18–20, 43:19–20 and 51:3. Here creation's renewal and the healing of people go together.
sections.refs: Isaiah 32:15–18; Isaiah 33:9; Isaiah 35:1–10; Isaiah 41:18–20; Isaiah 51:3; Revelation 21:1–4

sections.h: A new exodus in Isaiah 31 and 35
sections.b: Isaiah reaches for the exodus to describe new rescues. The LORD will "pass over" Jerusalem (31:5), using the verb of Exodus 12:13, and later tradition placed Sennacherib's defeat on Passover night. In chapter 35 the redeemed and the ransomed walk home through the wilderness on a holy road, with water in the desert, and no lion on the way (35:6–10). The words for "redeemed" (ge'ulim) and "ransomed" (peduyim) are exodus words, and the same picture of a highway in the desert returns in 40:3, 43:19 and 51:10–11.
sections.refs: Isaiah 31:5; Isaiah 35:6–10; Exodus 12:13; Isaiah 40:3; Isaiah 43:19; Isaiah 51:10–11

sections.b: Babylon's fall had already been announced in Isaiah 13–14 and 21:9, but in chapter 39 Babylon appears as a small, friendly power. Merodach-baladan, Assyria's great Babylonian rebel, sends envoys to Hezekiah, who shows them all his treasures (39:1–2). Isaiah's response names Babylon for the first time as the power that will carry off the palace's wealth and some of the king's descendants (39:6–7). The prophecy was fulfilled in 597 and 586 BC (2 Kings 24:13–15; 25:13–17), and the next chapter of Isaiah speaks comfort to Jerusalem after that exile (40:1–2).
sections.refs: Isaiah 39:1–8; Isaiah 13:19; Isaiah 21:9; Isaiah 40:1–2; 2 Kings 20:12–19; 2 Kings 24:13–15

sections.b: Hezekiah's prayer (Isaiah 37:16–20) is one of the Bible's clearest early statements that the LORD alone is God. He is "God, and you alone, over every kingdom on earth," the maker of heaven and earth; the gods Assyria destroyed were "no gods at all, only things that human hands had made out of wood and stone." The prayer asks for rescue so that "every kingdom on earth will know that you are the LORD, you alone." In the book of Isaiah it prepares for the argument of chapters 40–48: "I am the LORD, and there is no one else" (45:5).

sections.h: The Great Isaiah Scroll in Isaiah 31–39
sections.b: The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) is complete for these chapters and shows many small differences from the Masoretic Text: "witnesses" for "cities" (33:8), "his mouth" for "my mouth" (34:16), an added line in 34:4, readings that agree with 2 Kings in chapters 36–39 (36:5; 37:20; 37:25; 38:6), and, in 38:8, "the upper room of Ahaz." The scroll has a break after 33:24, with three blank lines, and chapter 34 begins a new column; many scholars think a second scribe began there. In the second half, later hands filled several gaps, including 38:21–22, which some take as evidence that those verses were added to Isaiah from Kings and others as an accidental omission later restored.
sections.refs: Isaiah 33:8; Isaiah 34:4; Isaiah 34:16; Isaiah 37:20; Isaiah 38:8; Isaiah 38:21–22

sections.b: Isaiah 36–39 tells of two prayers by Hezekiah, each answered at once. Facing Sennacherib's letter, he spreads it out before the LORD in the temple and prays that every kingdom will know the LORD alone is God (37:14–20); Isaiah's reply begins, "Because you prayed to me" (37:21). Facing death, he turns his face to the wall, reminds God of his faithful life and weeps; the LORD answers, "I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears" (38:2–5). His psalm (38:9–20) turns the answered prayer into praise. Chapter 33 also includes the people's prayer, "LORD, show us grace" (33:2).
sections.refs: Isaiah 33:2; Isaiah 37:14–21; Isaiah 38:2–5; Isaiah 38:9–20; 2 Kings 19:14–20; 2 Kings 20:2–5

sections.h: The LORD as judge, commander and king
sections.b: Isaiah 32–33 sets two kinds of kingship side by side. A human king will reign for righteousness, and his officials for justice, as shelter for the people (32:1–2). Then the people will see "a king in his beauty" (33:17), and the chapter ends: "For the LORD is our judge, / the LORD is our commander, / the LORD is our king. / He is the one who will save us" (33:22). The KJV's "lawgiver" in that verse is sometimes said to have inspired the three branches of the United States government, a claim with no support in the founders' writings.
